The faded label on the tin of tea, a pale yellow whisper of a forgotten afternoon, seems to hold the quiet warmth of a long-absent keeper. It is a small, tangible link to the human hands that once tended this tower, a reminder that even the most enduring structures carry the imprint of their caretakers. The stove, cold and its chimney sealed against the elements, stands as a silent witness to the passage of time, a relic of a life that once filled these cramped, low rooms with the rhythm of the sea.

The hand-drawn maps, with their imperfect lines and the stories attached to each inlet, speak to a different kind of patience and connection. They were not products of precision, but of a deep, personal engagement with the coast. Each measurement, each recorded detail, was infused with a sense of place that a sterile, automated view could never capture. This kind of attention, this willingness to see the world with a human eye, is what gave the coast its soul, and it is what the tower, in its stillness, continues to embody.
